# AI Agent-Assisted MicroDuck Walking Training: From Task Description to Policy

NVIDIA demonstrated how to transform task descriptions into robot simulation experiments: the agent plans around obstacles, creates assets, assembles scenes, and then uses reinforcement learning to train the MicroDuck’s motion strategy. This tutorial explains this process step by step and provides a training interface for public walking baselines. The images and animations in this article come from [ NVIDIA technical articles ](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/using-ai-agents-to-teach-robots-like-microduck-to-walk-in-simulation), and the video is from NVIDIA, showcasing NVIDIA’s demonstration.

[![Watch the full NVIDIA video: From task description to MicroDuck walking ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microduck-labels-1024x576-jpg.webp)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VvJai6HGfyE)

**[ Watch the full video by NVIDIA: From Prompt to Walking Robot With NVIDIA RTX Spark](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VvJai6HGfyE)**

## What happened between a single sentence and the training results

![NVIDIA's MicroDuck obstacle course and obstacle markings ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microduck-labels-1024x576-jpg.webp)

*NVIDIA concept diagram: Slopes, platforms, and other obstacles form the training environment for the robot.*

![ from planning, modeling, scene assembly to training and validation process ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microduck-Diagram.webp)

*NVIDIA flowchart: local planning and asset creation, cloud training, local validation, and real robot deployment preparation.*

The task description specifies what needs to be done; the agent breaks down the requirements into a plan and utilizes modeling and simulation tools. Reinforcement learning is responsible for generating the movement policy: the simulator drives the physical world based on actions, and the training algorithm updates the policy through multiple attempts and rewards. NVIDIA’s demonstration starts with a ready-made MicroDuck walking environment and pre-trained policies, followed by additional visual and obstacle motion training.

### 1. Break the task into scenario solutions

NVIDIA uses Hermes and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt to organize projects on RTX Spark. During the planning phase, it is necessary to review the models, capabilities, and constraints of MicroDuck, and then determine the route, obstacle sizes, passage space, and required output. The original example requires the creation and testing of a simulation obstacle field containing motion and navigation challenges; the prompt also describes steps such as concept mapping, asset recognition, modeling handover, and verification [. The full text of the ](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/using-ai-agents-to-teach-robots-like-microduck-to-walk-in-simulation) example is available in the first section of the original document.

![ Concept Diagram of Obstacle Field and Asset List ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot-Obstacles.webp)

*NVIDIA concept diagram and asset list: Identify reusable assets from objects such as ramps and platforms.*

After generating the concept diagram, the agent recognition map will be planned to identify different objects, merge duplicate instances, and retain names, positions, and reference cutouts for each asset type. Backs, dimensions, and occluded areas not visible in the image need to be recorded as assumptions. The planning, robot data, concept diagram, list, and execution requirements will then be packaged and handed over to Astra, who is responsible for asset production.

![ Plan the agent to generate an asset list and hand it over to ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Plan-inventory-generation-1.webp)

*NVIDIA demo: Organize task descriptions, concept diagrams, and asset lists into materials needed for subsequent modeling.*

### 2. Create assets suitable for simulation

The cropped reference image may be very small. NVIDIA's process first uses cloud-based image editing to organize the object reference, and then compares the contour, proportions, and colors with the original image. Astra arranges a locally running FreeCAD to create editable geometric structures, adds details and materials using Blender, and finally saves the model and exports the USD assets.

![FreeCAD modeling, Blender materials and generated work lights ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/FreeCADBlender.webp)

*NVIDIA demonstration: from geometric modeling in FreeCAD, to materials in Blender, and finally to a completed work light.*

In addition to generating new objects, it is also possible to retrieve OpenUSD assets in [SimReady Central](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/simready-central-assets-robotics-ai-factories) that have simulation properties, and combine ready-made assets with newly created models. Beyond the geometric appearance, attributes such as mass, collision bodies, and friction determine how the object behaves in the simulation.

![MicroDuck and the generated ramp and obstacle assets ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Walking-Robot.webp)

*NVIDIA demo: MicroDuck in scenarios such as ramps, steps, boxes, and pads.*

### 3. Assembly Scenarios and Robots

Astra places assets in Isaac Sim to organize robots, ramps, and obstacles. The robot links, joints, and actuators together determine how the control signals drive movement; Newton simulates contact, motion, and balance, while Omniverse's rendering and sensor functions provide scene observation.

![Obstacle Training Ground Assembled by Isaac Sim ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Overview-User-Interface.webp)

*NVIDIA demo: Check the layout of MicroDuck, ramps, and other obstacles in Isaac Sim.*

This scenario provides the actions that the robot can perform, the physical feedback from obstacles and the ground, as well as simulation sensor data for assessing the situation ahead. During training, collisions, falls, and progress all become part of the environmental feedback.

### 4. Train perception and movement policies using parallel simulation

![ Robot Policy Learning Closed Loop ](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microduck-Policy-Learning-Loop.webp)

*NVIDIA’s learning closed loop: the depth and robot state enter the policy, action-driven simulation, and then generate the next observation.*

The experiment starts with the [MicroDuck walking example ](https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab/tree/0c10609fd76534ccee3ae3973625003d65085441/source/isaaclab_tasks/isaaclab_tasks/contrib/microduck) and pre-trained motion policies from Isaac Lab, and further trains policies that can navigate over slopes and obstacles. The adaptation task uses the depth of the head camera and robot state as observations; after the policy outputs actions, the physics engine calculates the motion and contact at the next moment, and the reinforcement learning algorithm updates the policy accordingly.

![NVIDIA MicroDuck Parallel Slope Training Animation](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microduck-parallel-training.gif)

*NVIDIA original animation: Multiple simulation ducklings practice concurrently on different slopes and platforms.*

NVIDIA reported that the visual impairment adaptation experiment used **4096 parallel environments and 1 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU**. A large number of environments can generate training experience simultaneously, and a single failure can also serve as feedback for policy updates.

### 5. Put the training policy back into scenario validation

The policy is continuously updated during the training phase; during the evaluation phase, a checkpoint is selected to run the policy in the scenario and observe its performance. NVIDIA should pay attention to whether the robot recognizes obstacles, adjusts its actions, and completes the route, while recording the locations of falls, collisions, and getting stuck. Based on these data, it will decide how to modify the environment or continue training in the next round.

![NVIDIA MicroDuck Obstacle Scene Evaluation Animation](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Simulation-Policy-Evaluation.gif)

*NVIDIA raw animation: Evaluate the trained policy on the Isaac Sim obstacle field.*

### 6. Prepare to migrate from simulation to real robot

Real robot actuators suffer from delays, gear clearance issues, friction, and battery voltage fluctuations. Better Actuator Models (BAM) are used to simulate the response of these actuators during training; domain randomization changes physical parameters and observation noise during training, allowing the policy to experience a wider range of operating conditions. NVIDIA’s article covers deployment preparation and demonstrates the real robot performance of another Isaac Lab walking policy.

![NVIDIA MicroDuck Real Robot Walking Animation](https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microduck-Physical-Walking.gif)

*NVIDIA original animated video: The policy for the physical MicroDuck to run the walking strategy trained by Isaac Lab.*

[Microduck Simulation Training and Real Robot Deployment Guide](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/microduck-isaac-lab-sim-to-real) covers model export and onboard operation methods. The complete scene assets, visual policy weights, and training configurations for the NVIDIA obstacle demonstration have not been verified to form a fully reproducible release package; let’s start with the publicly available walking baseline first.

## Open Source Baseline: Isaac Lab Walk

[NVIDIA and Hugging Face's Microduck training tutorial ](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/microduck-isaac-lab-sim-to-real) provides tasks for walking on flat and rough surfaces. Here, [Isaac Lab's fixed submission 0c10609 ](https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab/tree/0c10609fd76534ccee3ae3973625003d65085441) is used as a code reference, and [ task registration ](https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab/blob/0c10609fd76534ccee3ae3973625003d65085441/source/isaaclab_tasks/isaaclab_tasks/contrib/microduck/__init__.py) includes two tasks: Flat and Rough; the upstream repository uses the BSD-3-Clause license. The upstream code link is provided here; its implementation is not copied.

The rough baseline includes slopes, steps, and random terrain; the current code indicates it is a visual-free speed walking task, and the foot height ray does not enter the actor observation. Therefore, it is suitable for reproduction of walking training but cannot be directly used as a depth vision obstacle avoidance policy in NVIDIA demonstrations. For flat and rough ground tasks, a 61-dimensional policy observation and a 14-dimensional joint target action are used; when publishing the policy, the observation order, normalization, and action scaling also need to be aligned.

### Environment and Training

1. Requires Linux, supported NVIDIA GPU and drivers, Git, and uv. The specific versions and hardware requirements are subject to [Isaac Lab installation documentation ](https://isaac-sim.github.io/IsaacLab/main/source/setup/installation/index.html). The following are the steps for using a fixed source version in an independent working directory:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
cd IsaacLab
git checkout 0c10609fd76534ccee3ae3973625003d65085441
uv sync
uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets
```

The list should include Flat and Rough tasks; when the tasks are not found, first check the code version and dependency installation. Start the rough ground training according to the upstream tutorial:

```bash
uv run isaaclab train \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
  --num_envs 4096 \
  presets=backlash
```

`presets=backlash` enables the actuator configuration with mechanical gaps; dynamic parameters are also randomized during training. 4096 is the number of parallel environments for the upstream tutorial, which should be adjusted according to the memory capacity; the training time and performance after reducing the number of parallel environments need to be measured again. The specific paths for the training logs and checkpoints depend on the running output.

### Playback and Export

After the training generates a checkpoint, use the upstream playback command in an environment with a graphical display:

```bash
uv run isaaclab play \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
  --checkpoint latest \
  --num_envs 16 \
  --viz newton_gl \
  presets=backlash
```

When replaying the upstream tutorial instructions, `exported/` used in that run will generate `policy.pt` and `policy.onnx`. Check the output to see if balance is maintained and the speed command is followed; record the number of falls, speed errors, performance on different terrains, and the video. For real robot ONNX deployment, a matching on-board interface must be used, and refer to [ Microduck deployment guide ](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/microduck-isaac-lab-sim-to-real#6-deploy-the-onnx-locomotion-policy-on-a-real-microduck).

## Connection with existing content in this topic

This topic already includes [MuJoCo walking HelloWorld](../../../../../16-专题组队学习/05-MicroDuck运动策略与任务开发专题/03-Notebook/00_MuJoCo策略控制_HelloWorld.ipynb), [basketball balance](../01-microduck-basketball-balance-reinforcement-learning/README.md), and multiple task training. First, use HelloWorld to understand the process of “observation → policy → joint goal → physical update”, then read the task configurations in Isaac Lab. This allows you to compare the observation, action, reward, and executor models of the two simulation training stacks. Visual obstacle avoidance requires additional camera observations, task definition, training configuration, and verifiable evaluation—it cannot be simply replaced by a single text instruction.
